newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka marks new year with peace elusive.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka marks new year with peace elusive.

text.p: Sri Lankans ushered in the new year somberly on Monday, praying for peace in the island ravaged by a 13-year-old ethnic war that has claimed thousands of lives.

Markets were closed and there was little traffic as majority Sinhalese and minority Tamils stayed home with families to play games, exchange greetings and prepare special meals for the new year before making a traditional visit to temples.

"The greatest challenge before us today is to achieve a lasting peace and prosperity. We possess the strength, capacity, strategy and tactics to take on successfully the challenges before us," President Chandrika Kumaratunga said in her New Year message.
Kumaratunga was referring to the war between government troops and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels.
The LTTE are fighting for an independent homeland for Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east. The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war. The LTTE says the toll is higher.

Hopes for peace were revived after Sri Lanka's two main political parties -- the ruling People'a Alliance and the main opposition United National party -- agreed this month to work together to end the ethnic war.

Speculation was rife ahead of new year celebrations that the government would announce a ceasefire as a concession to the rebels before reviving peace talks. But the government has denied any moves for negotiation.
Peace talks broke down in April 1995 when the LTTE sank two naval boats in eastern Trincomalee harbour.
"There is greater degree of optimism for peace this new year because of the agreement reached recently between the two major political parties," the independent Island newspaper said.
But at the same it warned the difficulty in predicting where such a consensus would lead, given the past rivalry between the two parties.
The state-owned Daily News called for political equality and power sharing between ethnic groups to ensure the survival of a united Sri Lanka.
"Only those war-ravaged societies which have thought even belatedly in terms of sharing political power and caring for each of its members have survived and won the day," it said.
"We in Sri Lanka too need to change our mindset on matters of governance."
The newspaper said people were tired of the war and were turning to astrologers for comfort. It said the trend was visible in the growing demand for astrological periodicals.
"The politician and the doomsday soothsayer seem to be ruling the popular mind in tandem," it said.
